The household id is deterministic: the first twelve hex characters of the SHA-256 digest 35 * of the normalized last name and the postcode joined by '|'. Owners that share a normalized 36 * last name and postcode therefore derive the same id automatically, without any explicit 37 * link. 38 */ 39 @Component 40 public class HouseholdResolver { 41 42 private final ClinicService clinicService; 43 44 public HouseholdResolver(ClinicService clinicService) { 45 this.clinicService = clinicService; 46 } 47 48 /** 49 * The stable, shared household identifier for {@code owner}: the first twelve hex 50 * characters of {@code SHA-256(normalizedLastName + '|' + postcode)}. "" : owner.getPostcode(); 58 String key = IdentityUtils.normalizeIdentity(owner.getLastName()) + "|" + postcode; 59 return HashUtils.sha256HexPrefix(key, 12); 60 } 61 62 /** 63 * Whether an existing owner already belongs to {@code owner}'s household, i.e. shares its 64 * computed household id (same normalized last name and postcode). Such a second owner is a 65 * household duplicate unless it deliberately declares {@code sharesHousehold}. 66 * 67 * @param owner the owner about to be created 68 * @return {@code true} if an already-registered owner shares this owner's household 69 */ 70 public boolean householdExists(Owner owner) { 71 String householdId = householdId(owner); 72 return this.clinicService.findAllOwners().stream() 73 .anyMatch(existing -> householdId.equals(householdId(existing))); 74 } 75 } 76

The telephone number of the pet owner. On create the value is
            normalized to E.164 form: spaces, dashes and brackets are stripped;
            a leading '+' and country code are kept when present, otherwise
            country code '+61' is assumed and a single leading '0' is dropped
            from the national digits. The stored and returned value is a '+'
            followed by 8 to 15 digits (e.g. '0412 345 678' becomes
            '+61412345678').
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 20
          example: '6085551023'
        email:
          title: Email address
          description: >-
            The email address of the pet owner. Optional. When supplied it must
            be a syntactically valid address and is stored and returned
            lower-cased.
          type: string
          format: email
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 255
          example: george.franklin@example.com
        registrationDate:
          title: Registration date
          description: >-
            The date the pet owner was registered. Optional on create; when not
            supplied it defaults to the server's current date. Returned in ISO
            'YYYY-MM-DD' format.
          type: string
          format: date
          example: '2020-06-15'
        birthDate:
          title: Birth date
          description: >-
            The pet owner's date of birth. Optional. When supplied it drives the
            derived 'ageBand'. Returned in ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' format.
          type: string
          format: date
          example: '1990-01-01'
        postcode:
          title: Postcode
          description: >-
            An optional 4-digit postcode. When supplied it must be valid for the
            owner's city per a fixed region table (NSW 2000-2099, VIC 3000-3099,
            QLD 4000-4099); a city with no known region accepts any 4-digit
            postcode. Stored and returned when given.
          type: string
          pattern: '^[0-9]{4}$'
          example: '2000'
        sharesHousehold:
          title: Shares household
          description: >-
            Write-only flag set on create to acknowledge that this owner
            deliberately shares a household with an existing owner. When true it
            allows creating an owner whose lastName and address match an existing
            owner instead of rejecting the request with 409.
          type: boolean
          writeOnly: true
          example: true

The build compiles and the test outcome is **identical to the baseline**: `functionalityStillAcceptsFlatAddress` passes; `coreNormalizesAndComposesStructuredAddress` remains the same 400 failure it was before I touched anything. My change altered no behaviour.

## Summary

I prepared the code for the structured-address change without implementing it.

**What I found.** The upcoming change concentrates on two named hotspots: `OwnerRestControllerV1.addOwner` and the `Owner` address accessors. The codebase has a strong, consistent idiom — each address-adjacent concern lives in a dedicated `@Component` (`AddressNormalizer`, `HouseholdResolver`, `CityRegionResolver`, `TelephoneNormalizer`), and inside `addOwner` every *derived-field computation* is extracted to a focused private helper (`customerCode`, `namesakeCount`, `possibleDuplicateOf`, `membershipNumber`), while the *normalize-and-validate* steps sit inline. The address step is the one about to grow substantially.

**What I changed.** In `OwnerRestControllerV1`, I extracted the inline address normalize-and-validate block into a single private helper, `normalizedAddress(owner)`, that delegates to `AddressNormalizer` and returns the canonical address or `null` when there is none — matching the existing `telephoneNormalizer.normalize(...) → null → 400` shape right below it. This:
- gives the "prefer structured fields, fall back to flat `address`, compose the stored string" logic one focused home to grow into, instead of ballooning inside the ~100-line `addOwner`;
- keeps that logic in the controller/normalizer seam rather than being crammed into the `Owner` entity's accessors — `Owner` stays the clean JavaBean it is today, which is the guard for the second named hotspot.

I deliberately did **not** add speculative structured-address methods/fields (they'd be dead code and would constitute implementing the change).

**One thing to flag honestly.** I could not "make all tests green."
